schema_notes.is_historical_867: True if the barony name is contemporarily attested as a settlement, fortress, or administrative unit by <= 867 CE.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: True if the barony name directly adopts a specific proper hydronym, oronym, choronym, or named topographic feature (excluding directional/locator compounds).
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Records attested pre-867 CE names for the same site or immediate predecessor when distinct from the barony name.

b_guidimaka.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Guidimakha (Gidimaxa) is recorded in Soninke oral tradition and later colonial-era ethnography as a Soninke dyamare (chiefdom) in southern Mauritania and western Mali.
b_guidimaka.etymology_analysis: From Soninke Gidimaxa, the indigenous name of a Soninke chiefdom (dyamare) in the upper Senegal River valley and Assaba foothills; often folk-etymologized in Soninke oral tradition as referring to rock/stone or early Soumaré/Kamara founders.

current_repo_state.name: Guidimake
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Guidimake).

b_diafunu.first_mention_attestation: First attested in written Arabic sources as Zāfqū / Zāfūn by al-Bakri in 1068 CE (Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik), and subsequently by al-Idrisi (1154 CE) and Yaqut al-Hamawi (1220 CE).

morphemes.translation: Dia (ancestral town in the Inner Niger Delta)

b_diafunu.etymology_analysis: Soninke Diafunu (Dyahunu), meaning 'people of Dia', referring to a Soninke dyamare centered on the upper Kolinbiné River in western Mali; rendered in medieval Arabic as Zāfūn.

b_karakoro.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; documented in 19th–20th century French colonial geography and hydrography as a right-bank tributary of the Senegal River.
b_karakoro.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Karakoro River, an intermittent right-bank tributary of the Senegal River forming part of the Mali–Mauritania border; the name is of local Soninke/Mande origin.

b_nioro.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Kingui (the Pulaar name for the Diarra/Diawara kingdom centered around Nioro) is recorded in post-medieval Sahelian oral traditions and 19th-century colonial accounts.

morphemes.translation: Kingui (regional name for the Diarra/Nioro territory)

b_nioro.etymology_analysis: Pulaar regional designation (Kingi / Kingui) applied to the Soninke Kingdom of Diarra (founded 11th century CE) in northwestern Mali around Nioro du Sahel.

current_repo_state.name: Kingui
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kingui).

b_kingui.first_mention_attestation: Unattested historically; 'Elisabethstat' is a fictional German-style disambiguated municipal name generated in the repository for an intra-county holding.
b_kingui.etymology_analysis: Fictional repository compound combining the European personal name Elisabeth with archaic German stat ('town/city'), used as a synthetic disambiguation for a second holding in c_kingui.

current_repo_state.name: Elisabethstat
current_repo_state.b_origin: Elisabethstat — Disambiguated capital foundation: Municipal foundation chartered by Elisabeth
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_yelimane.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Yélimané appears in 18th–19th century Kaarta Bambara and French colonial records (e.g., captured by a French column in December 1890 CE).
b_yelimane.etymology_analysis: Local Soninke settlement name in the Guidimé/Diafounou region of western Mali, recorded in 19th-century Kaarta and French colonial history.

current_repo_state.name: Jelimane
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Jelimane).

b_sorma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Sorma (also Soroma) is documented only in modern Malian administrative geography (Kayes Region).
b_sorma.etymology_analysis: Modern Malian local settlement name in the Kayes Region (Bafoulabé/Diéma area), without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_sero.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Sero (Sero Diamanou) is documented only in modern Malian administrative geography in the Kayes Region.
b_sero.etymology_analysis: Local Soninke/Khassonké village name in the Kayes Region of western Mali, unattested in medieval written sources.

b_farabugu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Kaarta is first attested in Songhai/Timbuktu chronicle traditions for 1502 CE (when Askia Muhammad I sacked a royal residence in Kaarta), and rose as a Bambara kingdom in the 17th–18th centuries CE.
b_farabugu.etymology_analysis: Historical region of western Mali between the upper Senegal and Niger basins, associated with the 17th–19th century Bambara Massassi Kingdom of Kaarta.

current_repo_state.name: Kârte
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kârte).

b_gemukura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Guémoukoura is attested in 19th-century Umarian and French colonial sources (occupied by Bamana forces in 1870 CE and site of the Battle of Guémoukoura in 1872 CE).
b_gemukura.etymology_analysis: Bambara compound meaning 'New Guémou' (Guémou + koura 'new'), referring to the 19th-century fortress south of Kaarta.

b_diara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Kaniaga (Khaniaga) appears in post-medieval oral traditions of the Sosso Empire (12th–13th centuries CE) and 19th–20th century historiography.

morphemes.translation: north / northern land (between upper Senegal and Niger bend)

b_diara.etymology_analysis: Soninke/Malinke historical region name (Kaniaga / Khaniaga), derived from a Malinke term meaning 'north', applied to the region north of Manden where the Sosso Empire arose.

current_repo_state.name: Kaniage
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kaniage).

b_kaniaga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested historically; 'Brunhildestat' is a fictional German-style disambiguated municipal name generated in the repository for an intra-county holding.
b_kaniaga.etymology_analysis: Fictional repository compound combining the Germanic personal name Brunhilde with archaic German stat ('town/city'), used as a synthetic disambiguation for a second holding in c_kaniaga.

current_repo_state.name: Brunhildestat
current_repo_state.b_origin: Brunhildestat — Disambiguated capital foundation: Municipal foundation chartered by Brunhilde
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_bakunu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Bakounou (Bakhunu) is recorded in Soninke oral traditions of the Ghana/Wagadu Empire and 19th–20th century French colonial ethnography.
b_bakunu.etymology_analysis: Traditional Soninke province name (Bakhunu / Bakounou) in the Nara/Goumbou region of Mali, south of the Hodh.

b_kita.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Kita is attested in Mali Empire historical traditions (associated with Mansa Maghan Keita II, also called Kita Tenin Maghan Keita, c. 1387 CE, and Ibn Khaldun's late 14th-century accounts) and later 19th-century French colonial records.

morphemes.translation: Kita (town and mountain massif in western Mali)

b_kita.etymology_analysis: Malinke toponym for the historic town and province at the eastern foot of Mount Kita in western Mali.

current_repo_state.name: Kite
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kite).

b_birgo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Birgo is documented in 19th-century French colonial records (e.g., the French protectorate of Birgo in 1882 CE around Mourgoula) and 20th-century archival studies.
b_birgo.etymology_analysis: Historical Malinke/Fula chiefdom and colonial canton south of Kita in western Mali, centered around Mourgoula.

b_bangasi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Bangassi near Kita is documented in 19th–20th century French colonial archives of Mali.
b_bangasi.etymology_analysis: Local Malinke/Khassonké settlement name in the Kayes/Kita region of western Mali, unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_banamba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Sosso (Soso) kingdom flourished in the 12th–13th centuries CE and is recorded in the Epic of Sundiata and Ibn Khaldun's late 14th-century history.

morphemes.translation: horse (traditional etymology linked to Sosso horse-trade monopoly)

b_banamba.etymology_analysis: Name of the 12th–13th century Soninke kingdom of Sosso (Soso) and its capital near Boron in Koulikoro Region, Mali; traditionally linked to the Mande word for 'horse'.

current_repo_state.name: Sosô
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Sosô).

b_kolokani.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Kolokani is documented in modern Malian and French colonial geography of the Bélédougou region.
b_kolokani.etymology_analysis: Bambara town name in the Bélédougou region of Koulikoro, Mali, unattested in medieval written sources.

b_lanba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Lanba is a local Malian toponym without pre-867 CE written attestation.
b_lanba.etymology_analysis: Local Mande settlement name in western/central Mali, without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_kouga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Kouga is documented only as a modern Malian locality name.
b_kouga.etymology_analysis: Local Malian toponym in the Middle Niger / Lakes region, unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

current_repo_state.name: Kouge
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kouge).

b_ras_el-ma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Ra's al-Mā' ('Head of the Water') is first attested in Arabic by al-Bakri in 1068 CE and later in the Tarikh al-Sudan (17th century CE) in connection with Sonni Ali's 1480s canal project.
b_ras_el-ma.etymology_analysis: Arabic Ra's al-Mā' ('Head of the Water'), referring to the western hydrographic extremity of Lake Faguibine in northern Mali.

b_tondiaru.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the megalithic site of Tondidarou (dated archaeologically to 670–790 CE) was first recorded in writing by Jules Brévié in 1904 CE.
b_tondiaru.etymology_analysis: Songhay toponym (Tondidarou / Tondiaru) referring to the standing phalliform stone megaliths on Lake Takadji near Niafunké; the archaeological site dates to c. 670–790 CE, but the name is not contemporarily attested in writing until 1904 CE.

b_dia.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Macina (Massina) is attested in Timbuktu chronicles (Tarikh al-Sudan) for events from c. 1400–1477 CE onward (e.g., the Sultanate of Massina and Mossi raids in 1477 CE).

morphemes.translation: Macina (Inner Niger Delta region and polity)

b_dia.etymology_analysis: Fula/Soninke name (Maasina / Macina) for the Inner Niger Delta region and the c. 1400 CE Sultanate of Massina in central Mali.

current_repo_state.name: Massine
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Massine).

b_mara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Dia-Mara is an archaeological mound in the Dia settlement complex (occupied from the 6th century CE) documented in 20th-century archaeology.

morphemes.translation: Mara (mound site in the Dia complex)

b_mara.etymology_analysis: Modern archaeological and local name for Dia-Mara, one of the three settlement mounds of the Dia complex in the Inner Niger Delta, Mali.

b_shoma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Dia-Shoma is an archaeological mound in the Dia complex (occupied from the 9th–6th century BCE) documented in 20th-century archaeology.

morphemes.translation: Shoma (oldest mound site in the Dia complex)

b_shoma.etymology_analysis: Modern archaeological and local name for Dia-Shoma, the largest and oldest mound (49 ha) of the Dia complex in the Inner Niger Delta, Mali.

b_kolima.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Méma appears in the oral Epic of Sundiata (13th century CE) and in 15th–17th century Timbuktu chronicles (conquered by Songhai in 1465 CE).

morphemes.translation: Méma (alluvial plain and former Soninke kingdom)

b_kolima.etymology_analysis: Soninke choronym for the alluvial basin west of Lake Debo and the Inner Niger Delta, and the Soninke constituent kingdom of the Ghana and Mali empires.

current_repo_state.name: Meme
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Meme).

b_akumbu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Akumbu mound complex in Méma (occupied archaeologically c. 400–1400 CE) is known only from 20th-century archaeological surveys.
b_akumbu.etymology_analysis: Local/archaeological name of the Akumbu iron-working and settlement mound complex in the Méma region of central Mali.

b_toladie.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Toladié (occupied archaeologically c. 430–670 CE) is known only from 20th-century archaeological surveys in Méma.
b_toladie.etymology_analysis: Local/archaeological name of Toladié, a 76-hectare iron-age occupation site in the Méma basin of Mali.

b_boulel.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Boulel is known only from modern archaeological surveys of iron-producing sites in Méma.

morphemes.translation: Boulel (settlement and iron-smelting site in Méma)

b_boulel.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name in the Méma region of Mali, documented in modern archaeological literature as an iron-smelting community.

b_west_mema.first_mention_attestation: Unattested historically; 'West-Méma' is a modern directional compound created in the repository.
b_west_mema.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound combining English 'West' with the Soninke choronym Méma.

current_repo_state.name: West-Meme
current_repo_state.b_origin: Western marshes of the ancient pre-867 Soninke kingdom of Méma (in-game: West Mema)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English descriptor West Mema fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; standardized to West-Meme.

b_awdaghost.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Arabic geographical term al-Ḥawḍ ('the Basin') for this Mauritanian depression is post-medieval/modern.
b_awdaghost.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-ḥawḍ ('basin', 'water trough'), designating the vast sedimentary depression (Hodh) of southeastern Mauritania.

current_repo_state.name: Hodh
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Hodh).

b_hodh_south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested historically; 'Zant-Ganiya' is a fictional disambiguated church holding name generated in the repository.
b_hodh_south.etymology_analysis: Fictional repository compound combining a Germanic/Dutch-style 'Zant' ('Saint') prefix with 'Ganiya' to disambiguate a church holding in c_hodh.

current_repo_state.name: Zant-Ganiya
current_repo_state.b_origin: Zant-Ganiya — Disambiguated capital foundation: Patron saint church dedicated by Ganiya
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_hodh_west.first_mention_attestation: Unattested historically as a medieval name; 'West-Hodh' is a modern directional compound (paralleling modern Hodh El Gharbi).
b_hodh_west.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound combining English 'West' with Arabic al-ḥawḍ ('basin').

current_repo_state.name: West-Hodh
current_repo_state.b_origin: Western basin of the ancient pre-867 Hodh depression (in-game: Hodh-West)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English descriptor Hodh-West fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; standardized to West-Hodh.

b_tagant.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Tagant is documented in post-medieval Mauritanian oral history and French colonial geography.
b_tagant.etymology_analysis: From Zenaga Berber tagant ('forest'), applied as an oronym to the stony Tagant Plateau of south-central Mauritania.

current_repo_state.name: Tagant
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Tagant).

b_tagant_west.first_mention_attestation: Unattested historically; 'Tagant West' is a modern directional compound for an unoccupied holding.
b_tagant_west.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound combining the Berber oronym Tagant with English 'West'.

b_tichitt.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the oasis town of Tichitt was traditionally founded c. 1150 CE (6th century AH) and is recorded in Mauritanian chronicles and UNESCO heritage historiography.

morphemes.translation: Tichitt (oasis town at the foot of the Tagant Plateau)

b_tichitt.etymology_analysis: Berber toponym (Ticit / Tichitt) for the historic ksar and oasis town in south-central Mauritania, adjacent to the Neolithic Dhar Tichitt escarpment.

current_repo_state.name: Titschitt
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Titschitt).

b_akrijit.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Akreijit is a modern Mauritanian town near the Neolithic Dhar Tichitt archaeological sites.
b_akrijit.etymology_analysis: Local Hassaniya Arabic/Berber name of a town in the Tagant region of central Mauritania, known archaeologically for nearby Neolithic Tichitt-tradition rock art.

b_al-ghaba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Awkar (Aouker) is documented in Mauritanian oral traditions of Wagadu and modern geography.

morphemes.translation: Aouker (basin and dune region of southern Mauritania)

b_al-ghaba.etymology_analysis: Regional choronym (Awkar / Aouker) for the endorheic basin and dune landscape of southeastern Mauritania, core homeland of the Ghana/Wagadu Empire.

current_repo_state.name: Awkar
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Awkar).

b_niara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Niara is documented only as a modern locality in the Mauritania–Mali borderland.
b_niara.etymology_analysis: Local toponym in the Hodh/Wagadu borderland between Mauritania and Mali, without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_bou_khzama.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Bou Khzama is a modern Mauritanian locality and archaeological site (DN4) in Dhar Néma.
b_bou_khzama.etymology_analysis: Hassaniya Arabic toponym (Bū Khzāma, 'place of lavender/desert herb') in Hodh Ech Chargui, Mauritania, where Neolithic/Iron Age remains have been excavated.

b_kumbi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; the name Qunbi (Koumbi) is first attested in the 17th-century Timbuktu chronicle Tarikh al-Fattash (c. 1665 CE), whereas earlier Arabic authors (al-Bakri 1068 CE) referred to the capital simply as Ghāna.

morphemes.translation: Koumbi (capital settlement of the Ghana Empire)

b_kumbi.etymology_analysis: Soninke name (Qunbi / Koumbi) for the archaeological city of Koumbi Saleh in southeastern Mauritania, widely identified as a capital of the Ghana Empire.

older_name_by_867.notes: Early Arabic geographers referred to the capital/realm of the Ghana Empire simply as Ghāna before Qunbi (Koumbi) was recorded in Tarikh al-Fattash (c. 1665 CE).

b_gumbu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Goumbou (traditionally linked to 7th-century Soninke foundation legends) is recorded only in post-medieval oral tradition and 19th-century colonial accounts.
b_gumbu.etymology_analysis: Soninke town name (Goumbou / Gumbu) in the Ouagadou commune near Nara, Mali.

b_kedama.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Masin is unattested in medieval Arabic sources.
b_kedama.etymology_analysis: Local toponym in the Wagadu/Hodh region, unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

current_repo_state.name: Masin
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Masin).

b_masin.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Masin is unattested in medieval Arabic sources.
b_masin.etymology_analysis: Local toponym in the Wagadu/Hodh region, unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_timbedra.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Timbedra was founded c. 1904 CE during the French colonial period by members of the Ehel Med Mahmoud (Mechdhouf) family.
b_timbedra.etymology_analysis: Hassaniya Arabic/Berber name of a town in Hodh Ech Chargui, southeastern Mauritania, founded c. 1904 CE.

b_walata.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Oualata (Iwalatan / Walāta) is first attested in written sources by Ibn Battuta in 1352 CE, and later in 17th-century Timbuktu chronicles.
b_walata.etymology_analysis: Oasis town in southeastern Mauritania; derived either from Berber Iwalatan or Arabized from Malinke wala ('shady place') after the 15th–17th centuries CE.

current_repo_state.name: Walate
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Walate).

b_biru_walata.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Biru (Bīru, the earlier Soninke name for Oualata) is attested in 17th-century Timbuktu chronicles such as Tarikh al-Sudan (c. 1655 CE).
b_biru_walata.etymology_analysis: Soninke name Bīru (plural of bire, 'open-sided structure/shelter'), the earlier Mande name of the oasis town later Arabized as Walata.

b_awgham.first_mention_attestation: Unattested by 867 CE; Awgham is first attested by Ibn Hawqal in 977 CE (recording Awdaghust's conquest of Awgham in 962 CE).
b_awgham.etymology_analysis: Medieval Sahelian polity/town name recorded in 10th-century Arabic geography (Ibn Hawqal 977 CE), located between Awdaghust and the Niger/Ghana.

b_bura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Bura archaeological site in southwest Niger (dated to c. 200–1300 CE) was only discovered in 1975 CE and excavated from 1983 CE.

morphemes.translation: Bura (modern village and archaeological site in Niger)

b_bura.etymology_analysis: Name of a modern village in Tillabéry Region, Niger, which gave its name to the 3rd–13th century CE Bura archaeological culture.

b_gabou_bura.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Gabou in the Bura/Téra region of Niger is documented only in modern geography.
b_gabou_bura.etymology_analysis: Local Nigerien settlement name in the Téra/Bura area, without pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_bilanga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Gurma (Gourma / Gulmu) appears in Songhai/Timbuktu chronicles (Tarikh al-Sudan, 17th century CE) and Mossi-Gourmantché oral traditions.

morphemes.translation: right bank of the Niger River / Gourma region

b_bilanga.etymology_analysis: Songhay/regional choronym (Gourma / Gurma) denoting the right-bank region south of the Niger Bend (modern eastern Burkina Faso and western Niger).

current_repo_state.name: Gurme
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Gurme).

b_sirba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Sirba River is documented in 19th–20th century colonial and modern West African hydrography.

morphemes.translation: Sirba (right-bank tributary of the Niger River)

b_sirba.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Sirba River, flowing from eastern Burkina Faso into the Niger River upstream of Niamey.

b_tondikwarey.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Tondikwarey is a modern Zarma/Songhay toponym in western Niger.
b_tondikwarey.etymology_analysis: Zarma/Songhay compound meaning 'White Rock' (tondi 'stone/rock' + kwarey 'white'), a settlement name in western Niger.

b_gurma-west.first_mention_attestation: Unattested historically; 'Gurma-West' is a modern directional compound for an unoccupied holding.
b_gurma-west.etymology_analysis: Modern directional compound combining the regional name Gurma with English 'West'.

b_nungu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Nungu (Noungou, indigenous name of Fada N'Gourma) is recorded in post-medieval Gourmantché/Mossi oral tradition and 19th-century colonial accounts.
b_nungu.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Gourmantché/Mossi name (Nungu / Nũngu) of Fada N'Gourma, capital of the Gourma region in eastern Burkina Faso.

b_tenkudugo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Tenkodogo is traditionally dated by oral history to c. 1100 CE as the earliest Mossi kingdom, and recorded in colonial-era writing.
b_tenkudugo.etymology_analysis: Mooré compound meaning 'Ancient Land' (ten- 'land' + kudugo 'ancient'), capital of the historic Mossi kingdom of Tenkodogo in Burkina Faso.

b_say.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Say on the Niger River rose in the 19th century CE as an Islamic scholarly center founded by Alfa Mohamed Diobo.

morphemes.translation: Say (town on the Niger River in southwestern Niger)

b_say.etymology_analysis: Town on the Niger River in Tillabéry Region, Niger, historically prominent from the 19th century CE.

current_repo_state.name: Say
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Say).

b_burunfongo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Burunfongo is a local toponym in the Niger–Burkina Faso borderland without medieval written attestation.
b_burunfongo.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name in the Lower Gurma / Niger River borderland, unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_aribinda.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; the Kurumba (Fulsé) people and Aribinda are documented in 19th-century colonial treaties (1895 CE) and 20th-century ethnography.

morphemes.translation: Kurumba (indigenous people of northern Burkina Faso)

b_aribinda.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Kurumba (Koromba / Fulsé), an ancient indigenous Gur-speaking population of northern Burkina Faso.

current_repo_state.name: Kurumbe
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kurumbe).

b_burzanga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Bourzanga (featuring a Kurumba royal necropolis) is documented only in 20th-century archaeology and modern Burkinabé geography.

morphemes.translation: Bourzanga (town in Bam Province, Burkina Faso)

b_burzanga.etymology_analysis: Town in Bam Province, northern Burkina Faso, noted for its Kurumba royal necropolis of 109 stelae.

b_mergao.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Mergao is a local settlement name in northern Burkina Faso without medieval written attestation.
b_mergao.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name in northern Burkina Faso (Kurumba/Upper Gurma area), unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_kissi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Oudalan is documented in post-medieval Tuareg/Fula history and modern Burkinabé administrative geography.

morphemes.translation: Oudalan (northernmost Sahelian region of Burkina Faso)

b_kissi.etymology_analysis: Regional choronym for the Oudalan province in the Sahel Region of northeastern Burkina Faso, bordering Mali and Niger.

current_repo_state.name: Oudalan
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Oudalan).

b_dinde.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources by 867 CE; Dinde is a local settlement name in the Oudalan/Sahel borderland without medieval written attestation.
b_dinde.etymology_analysis: Local toponym in the Oudalan/Upper Gurma borderland, unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.

b_oursi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; archaeological mound complexes around Oursi date to the 1st–2nd millennium CE, and the modern settlement is documented in colonial/post-colonial French West African records.

morphemes.translation: local toponym of Oudalan settlement and adjacent Mare d'Oursi

b_oursi.etymology_analysis: Oursi is a Sahelian toponym in Oudalan Province, northern Burkina Faso, associated with the adjacent Mare d'Oursi wetland and archaeological settlement mounds occupied during the 1st and early 2nd millennia CE before abandonment around 1400 CE.

b_saouga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; archaeological mound complexes at Saouga date to the 1st–2nd millennium CE, while written documentation of the commune is modern.
b_saouga.etymology_analysis: Saouga is a village and commune in Gorom-Gorom Department, Oudalan Province, Burkina Faso, known archaeologically for Iron Age settlement mounds occupied during the 1st to 14th centuries CE.

b_dori.first_mention_attestation: 1853 CE (visited and documented by Heinrich Barth during his Sahelian expedition; Dori served as capital of the Fula Emirate of Liptako founded in 1810 CE).

morphemes.translation: market town and capital of Liptako

b_dori.etymology_analysis: Dori is the historic capital of the Fula Emirate of Liptako (established 1810 CE) in northeastern Burkina Faso; its written attestation begins in 19th-century CE European travelogues such as Heinrich Barth's 1853 CE account.

b_gurma-rharous.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; 'Ôver-Gurme' is a reconstructed/Germanicized rendering of 'Upper Gurma' (after the Gurma/Gourmantché region and Gourma-Rharous on the Niger Bend, documented in post-867 Songhai and colonial sources).

morphemes.translation: Gurma (right-bank Niger Bend region and people)

b_gurma-rharous.etymology_analysis: Compound directional toponym meaning 'Upper Gurma', combining a reconstructed Germanic directional prefix with Gurma (the ethnonym/choronym for the Gourmantché region south of the Niger Bend). Excluded from natural_proper_name as a directional/locator compound.

current_repo_state.name: Ôver-Gurme
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Ôver-Gurme).

b_zampia.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Zampia is a modern archaeological designation (Zampia ceramic facies of the Windé Koroji Complex near Douentza, 1st millennium BCE, excavated 1993–1996 CE).

morphemes.translation: site name near Douentza in southern Gourma

b_zampia.etymology_analysis: Zampia is a modern archaeological site/facies name in the Windé Koroji Complex north of Douentza in southern Gourma, Mali, associated with first-millennium BCE pastoralist tumuli and stone alignments.

b_hombori.first_mention_attestation: Early 17th century CE (c. 1600s CE Songhai/Timbuktu chronicle traditions and Ahmad Baba's references to Hombori).

morphemes.translation: town at the foot of Hombori Tondo

b_hombori.etymology_analysis: Hombori (local Songhai Humburi) is a town in the Douentza area of central Mali situated beneath the Hombori Tondo massif; it became a refuge and strategic point for Songhai royal refugees after the 1591 CE Moroccan invasion.

b_bandiagara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Dogon settlement of the Bandiagara Escarpment dates from c. 14th–15th century CE, with written documentation in the 19th–20th century CE.
b_bandiagara.etymology_analysis: Derived from the archaic Dogon term bàndʒà-gàrá, meaning 'large wooden eating bowl', referring to ceremonial wooden bowls crafted by blacksmiths. The Dogon migrated to the escarpment around the 14th–15th century CE, succeeding the Tellem (11th–16th century CE).

current_repo_state.name: Bandiagare
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Bandiagare).

b_ounjougou.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Ounjougou is a modern lieu-dit discovered archaeologically in 1994 CE (with Paleolithic, Early Holocene pottery c. 9400 BCE, and pre-Dogon deposits).

morphemes.translation: local lieu-dit in the Upper Yamé Valley

b_ounjougou.etymology_analysis: Ounjougou is a Dogon lieu-dit in the Upper Yamé Valley on the Bandiagara Plateau, Mali, famous since 1994 CE excavations for yielding some of the earliest pottery in Africa (c. 9400 BCE) and a long pre-Dogon sequence.

b_douentza.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; the Séno-Gondo plain is documented in modern ethnographic and geographical literature.

morphemes.translation: sandy lowland plain southeast of the Bandiagara Escarpment

b_douentza.etymology_analysis: Gondô (Gondo) is the regional choronym for the Gondo plain (part of the Séno-Gondo plain) stretching southeast from the Bandiagara Escarpment toward Burkina Faso.

current_repo_state.name: Gondô
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Gondô).

b_samyere.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in the Gondo plain

b_samyere.etymology_analysis: Samyere is a local settlement name in the Gondo/Douentza area of central Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_bankass.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Séno (Seno) is documented in colonial and modern geographical/administrative records.
b_bankass.etymology_analysis: Senô (Séno) comes from Fulfulde séno ('sandy plain'), serving as the regional choronym for the Séno-Gondo plain at the foot of the Bandiagara Escarpment.

current_repo_state.name: Senô
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Senô).

b_douna.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in pre-modern written sources <= 867 CE; Douna (Douentza Cercle, Mopti Region) is a modern rural commune/village attested in 20th-century Malian administrative records (distinct from the homonymous Bani River hydrometric station).
b_douna.etymology_analysis: Douna is a village in central Mali (Douentza/Séno area, and also a homonymous hydrometric station on the Bani River recorded from 1922 CE), lacking pre-modern written attestation.

b_seno-south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; 'Sût-Senô' is a reconstructed directional compound ('South Séno').
b_seno-south.etymology_analysis: Directional compound meaning 'South Séno', combining a reconstructed Germanic directional prefix with Fulfulde séno ('sandy plain'). Excluded from natural_proper_name as a directional/locator compound.

current_repo_state.name: Sût-Senô
current_repo_state.b_origin: Southern plain of the pre-867 Séno-Gondo depression (in-game: Seno-South)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English descriptor Seno-South fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; standardized to Sût-Senô.

b_giti.first_mention_attestation: Mid-17th century CE (1655 CE Tarikh al-Sudan and 17th-century Tarikh al-fattash recounting 15th–16th century CE Songhai-Mossi conflicts; Kingdom of Yatenga founded in the 16th century CE).
b_giti.eponym_details: Named after Naaba Yadega (16th century CE), the Mossi prince who broke away from Ouagadougou to found the Kingdom of Yatenga (Mooré Yadega-tenga, 'land of Yadega').

morphemes.translation: personal name of the 16th-century Mossi founder Naaba Yadega

b_giti.etymology_analysis: Jatenge (Yatenga) derives from Mooré Yadega-tenga ('land of Yadega'), named after its 16th-century CE Mossi founder Naaba Yadega.

current_repo_state.name: Jatenge
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Jatenge).

b_walguyo.first_mention_attestation: 1757 CE (founded as Ouahigouya / Wayugyã by Naaba Kango as the capital of the Kingdom of Yatenga).

morphemes.translation: come and pay homage / bow down

b_walguyo.etymology_analysis: Walguyo represents Ouahigouya (Mooré Wayugyã), founded in 1757 CE by Naaba Kango as the capital of Yatenga; the Mooré name means 'come and pay homage'.

b_zondoma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Zondoma is a Mossi kingdom/province (traditionally founded by Rawa, son of Ouédraogo) documented in colonial and modern historical works.

morphemes.translation: historic Mossi polity and province centered on Gourcy

b_zondoma.etymology_analysis: Zondoma (also Zandoma) is a historic Mossi kingdom and modern province in northern Burkina Faso with its seat at Gourcy, documented in oral tradition and post-19th-century written historiography.

b_gursi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Gourcy (Gursi) was the early seat of Yatenga before 1757 CE and is documented in colonial/post-colonial records.

morphemes.translation: historic town and capital of Zondoma

b_gursi.etymology_analysis: Gursi (French Gourcy) is the historic Mossi town in Zondoma Province from which Yatenga rulers expanded in the 16th century CE before relocating the capital to Ouahigouya in 1757 CE.

b_rim.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; archaeological sites Rim I–III show occupation from c. 3000 BCE and ironworking in the 6th–10th centuries CE, while the village name is modern.

morphemes.translation: village and archaeological complex in Koumbri Department

b_rim.etymology_analysis: Rim is a village in Koumbri Department, Yatenga Province, Burkina Faso, notable archaeologically for the Rim I–III prehistoric and early iron-metallurgy sites (6th–10th centuries CE), though the toponym itself has no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_sanga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Dogon settlement at Sangha/Sanga dates to the 14th–15th centuries CE, and Sanga in Yatenga (Thiou) is documented in modern administrative records.

morphemes.translation: settlement name in Dogon Country / Yatenga

b_sanga.etymology_analysis: Sanga (Sangha in Mali, or Sanga in Thiou Department, Yatenga) is a regional settlement name; the Dogon cultural center of Sangha was settled around the 14th–15th centuries CE.

b_biun.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in eastern Burkina Faso

b_biun.etymology_analysis: Biun is a local toponym in the Gurma/Tapoa region of eastern Burkina Faso without documented pre-modern written attestation.

current_repo_state.name: Biun
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Biun).

b_gobnangou.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern geographical and administrative sources (including the 2025 CE Gobnangou Province reform).

morphemes.translation: sandstone cliff / escarpment range in southeastern Burkina Faso

b_gobnangou.etymology_analysis: Gobnangou is an oronym referring to the Chaîne de Gobnangou sandstone escarpment in southeastern Burkina Faso, which also gives its name to the surrounding province.

b_pentenga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Pentenga is a modern archaeological rock-shelter site in southeastern Burkina Faso.
b_pentenga.etymology_analysis: Pentenga is a rock-shelter archaeological site in southeastern Burkina Faso (alongside Yobri and Maadaga) known for Paleolithic/Holocene stone industries, lacking pre-modern written attestation.

b_bena.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern administrative and ethnographic records of the Bobo/Bwa region.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in the Bobo/Bwa region

b_bena.etymology_analysis: Bene (Béné / Bena) is a toponym in the Bobo/Bwa borderland between Mali and Burkina Faso without pre-modern written attestation.

current_repo_state.name: Bene
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Bene).

b_dourola.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; archaeological iron-smelting furnaces near Douroula date to the 8th century BCE, while the town name is documented in modern records.

morphemes.translation: town in Mouhoun Province, Burkina Faso

b_dourola.etymology_analysis: Dourola (Douroula) is a town in Mouhoun Province, western Burkina Faso, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List for nearby 8th-century BCE iron-smelting furnaces, though the town name is unattested in written sources <= 867 CE.

b_sikasso.first_mention_attestation: 1876 CE (made capital of the Kénédougou Kingdom by Tieba Traoré; besieged by Samori Touré in 1887–1888 CE and documented in French colonial records).
b_sikasso.etymology_analysis: Sikassô (Sikasso) in southern Mali incorporates the Manding element -so ('house/village') and rose to prominence only in 1876 CE as the fortified capital of the Kénédougou Kingdom.

current_repo_state.name: Sikassô
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Sikassô).

b_kumya.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in southern Mali

b_kumya.etymology_analysis: Kumya is a local settlement name in the Sikasso/Bobo borderland of southern Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_baninko.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Baninko is a historic Bambara region in Mali documented in modern ethnographic and historical literature.
b_baninko.etymology_analysis: Baninko is a historic Bambara region in Mali meaning 'beyond/behind the Bani (river)', a locator compound excluded from natural_proper_name.

b_soum.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Bindougou/Bendougou is documented in modern Malian geographical and administrative records.
b_soum.etymology_analysis: Bindugu (Bindougou / Bendougou) is a Bambara toponym combining dugu ('land/village') with bin ('grass'), without pre-modern written attestation.

current_repo_state.name: Bindugu
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Bindugu).

b_taba.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in the Bani/Ségou basin

b_taba.etymology_analysis: Taba is a local settlement name in the Bindugu/Ségou area of central Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_san.first_mention_attestation: 1690 CE (conquered by Biton Coulibaly of the Bamana Empire; earlier 1542 CE Songhai raid targeted 'Sama', which may refer to Sama Foulala rather than San).

morphemes.translation: market town near the Bani River

b_san.etymology_analysis: San is a historic market town in central Mali near the Bani River; local tradition links its founding to the sanké pond, toro fig tree, and karantéla well, and it entered written history in the 17th–19th centuries CE.

b_segou.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Do/Dodougou is attested in Mandinka oral traditions (Sunyata epic, 13th century CE) and modern historiography of pre-imperial Mali.
b_segou.etymology_analysis: Dodugu (Dodougou) means 'land of Do', referring to the northeastern constituent province of pre-imperial Manden (alongside Kri) ruled by the Konaté/Conté clan in Mandinka oral tradition.

current_repo_state.name: Dodugu
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Dodugu).

b_kri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kri/Kiri is attested in Mandinka oral traditions (13th century CE Sunyata epic) and modern historiography of the Mali Empire.
b_kri.etymology_analysis: Kri (Kiri) is one of the core constituent provinces of Manden (alongside Do/Dodougou) in the 13th-century CE Mali Empire formation traditions, associated with the Traoré clan.

b_niamina.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in colonial/modern Malian geographical records.

morphemes.translation: settlement name along the Niger River in Koulikoro/Ségou

b_niamina.etymology_analysis: Niamina is a riverine town in Mali along the Niger River between Koulikoro and Ségou, lacking pre-modern written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_tamani.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Malian administrative records.

morphemes.translation: small talking drum / town name in Barouéli Cercle

b_tamani.etymology_analysis: Tamani is a town and commune in Barouéli Cercle, Ségou Region, Mali (homonymous with the Bambara tamani talking drum), without pre-modern written attestation.

b_sanado.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in central Mali

b_sanado.etymology_analysis: Sanado is a local settlement name in the Ségou/Dodugu region of central Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_jenne-jeno.first_mention_attestation: 1447 CE (Antonio Malfante's Latin letter from Tuwat referring to 'Geni'; also 17th-century CE Tarikh al-Sudan; archaeological Jenné-Jeno dates from c. 250 BCE–900 CE without contemporary written attestation of the name).

morphemes.translation: historic trading city on the Bani floodplain

b_jenne-jeno.etymology_analysis: Dschenne (Germanized spelling of Djenné) is the famous Inland Niger Delta trading city; while its predecessor mound Jenné-Jeno was occupied from c. 250 BCE, the name Djenné ('Geni') is first attested in writing in 1447 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Dschenne
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Dschenne).

older_name_by_867.notes: Jenné-Jeno was archaeologically occupied c. 250 BCE–900 CE, but no contemporary pre-867 written source records its name.

b_kaniana.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kaniana is an archaeological tell near Djenné excavated in 1981 CE and inscribed as part of UNESCO's Old Towns of Djenné in 1988 CE.
b_kaniana.etymology_analysis: Kaniana is one of the four archaeological tell sites comprising the Old Towns of Djenné in the Inland Niger Delta, Mali, lacking pre-modern written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_mopti.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Mopti grew from a Bozo fishing village in the 19th–20th centuries CE.

morphemes.translation: gathering place / confluence settlement at the Niger-Bani junction

b_mopti.etymology_analysis: Mopti (Fulfulde Mobti) is located at the confluence of the Niger and Bani rivers in central Mali; it developed into a major town in the 19th–20th centuries CE without pre-modern written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_kiri-bara.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.
b_kiri-bara.etymology_analysis: Kiri-Bara is a compound toponym in the Inland Niger Delta / Djenné area of Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_korienza.first_mention_attestation: 1494 CE (creation of the office of Kurmina-fari by Askia Mohammad I of the Songhai Empire, recorded in 17th-century Timbuktu chronicles Tarikh al-Sudan and Tarikh al-fattash).

morphemes.translation: western provinces of the Songhai Empire south of Timbuktu

b_korienza.etymology_analysis: Kurmine (Kurmina) was the major western province of the Songhai Empire in the Inland Niger Delta / Niger Bend, governed by the Kurmina-fari from 1494 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Kurmine
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kurmine).

b_bangu.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: pond, floodplain depression, or local settlement

b_bangu.etymology_analysis: Bangu is a local Malian toponym in the Kurmina/Niger Bend area (cf. Songhai bangu 'pond/lake') without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_safare.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in the Inland Niger Delta

b_safare.etymology_analysis: Safare is a local settlement name in the Kurmina/Inland Niger Delta area of Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_nguma.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; no pre-modern written attestation found.

morphemes.translation: local settlement name in the Inland Niger Delta

b_nguma.etymology_analysis: Nguma is a local settlement name in the Kurmina/Inland Niger Delta area of Mali without documented pre-modern written attestation.

b_niamina_jara.first_mention_attestation: 1732 CE (recorded as 'Jagra' on Capt. John Leach's map of the River Gambia; Jarra was one of the Mandinka kingdoms on the south bank of the Gambia).

morphemes.translation: historic Mandinka kingdom on the south bank of the Gambia River

b_niamina_jara.etymology_analysis: Dschare (Germanized spelling of Jarra/Jara, formerly also written Jagra) was a Mandinka kingdom on the south bank of the Gambia River, first attested in 1732 CE cartography.

current_repo_state.name: Dschare
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Dschare).

b_kiang.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kiang is documented in post-16th-century European maps and colonial Gambian records as a Mandinka kingdom.

morphemes.translation: historic Mandinka kingdom on the south bank of the Gambia River

b_kiang.etymology_analysis: Kiang was a pre-colonial Mandinka kingdom on the south bank of the Gambia River (now Kiang West, Central, and East districts in The Gambia), attested only in early modern and colonial sources.

b_pakao.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Pakao is documented in Mandinka oral traditions, the Ajami Pakao Book, and colonial Senegalese records.

morphemes.translation: historic Mandinka province in middle Casamance

b_pakao.etymology_analysis: Pakao is a historic Mandinka cultural and Islamic scholarly region in the middle Casamance (Sédhiou region, Senegal), documented in post-medieval oral traditions and Ajami manuscripts.

b_achum.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE (established as a Portuguese trading post in the early 16th century CE along the Geba River, following mid-15th-century Portuguese coastal exploration).
b_achum.etymology_analysis: Gebe (Geba) is named after the Geba River; according to historical sources, 'Geba' derives from the Biafada term bejébi ('fresh water').

current_repo_state.name: Gebe
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Gebe).

b_birasu.first_mention_attestation: c. 1506 CE (Valentim Fernandes, Description de la Côte Occidentale d'Afrique, mentioning the faran of Birasu).

morphemes.translation: historic Mandinka-ruled kingdom between the Casamance and Cacheu rivers

b_birasu.etymology_analysis: Birasu (also Braço / Birassu) was a Mandinka kingdom in the Kaabu/Casamance sphere, first attested in writing around 1506 CE by Valentim Fernandes.

b_mansoa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; the Mansôa town grew from a 19th-century CE Portuguese trading post on the Mansoa River (permanent military post 1913 CE).

morphemes.translation: major river and town in central Guinea-Bissau

b_mansoa.etymology_analysis: Mansoa (Mansôa) is named after the Mansoa River in central Guinea-Bissau; the modern town developed from a 19th-century CE Portuguese trading post.

b_guinala.first_mention_attestation: 16th century CE (1583 CE Portuguese retreat to a fort at Guinala; also documented in late 16th-century CE accounts by André Álvares de Almada as a Biafada kingdom).

morphemes.translation: Biafada kingdom and port on the Rio Grande de Buba (also Quinara)

b_guinala.etymology_analysis: Guinala (also Quinara) was a major pre-colonial Biafada kingdom and trading port between the Geba and Rio Grande de Buba rivers, attested in 16th-century CE Portuguese sources.

b_kombo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Kombo/Jame is documented in post-15th-century European coastal accounts and colonial Gambian records.
b_kombo.etymology_analysis: Dschâm (Germanized rendering of Jame, paired with Kombo in western Gambia) represents a coastal Senegambian polity under Mali/Kaabu influence, attested only in early modern and colonial sources.

current_repo_state.name: Dschâm
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Dschâm).

b_fogny.first_mention_attestation: Late 16th century CE (c. 1594 CE André Álvares de Almada, Tratado Breve dos Rios de Guiné, mentioning the king of Fogni; earlier 15th-century Bainuk state).
